description: We are operating in Bristol and are taking part in the Martian Map challenge. Anyone who wish to join our team should be interested in the activity
summary:
Mars GIS: An Interplanetary Survival Guide
We are Year 10 students with little coding experience, so we focused on requirements elicitation: working out what a future Mars explorer needs from a map. We designed a GIS dashboard as a stack of layers (3D ground, surface skin, science overlays and clickable pins) with five themes: volcanoes, relief contours, ancient rivers and lakes, geology and minerals, and surface features like craters and rover tracks. Users control it with toggles, 1-101 sliders, zooming and clicking. Claude (Anthropic’s AI) coded it in HTML from our requirements; we made the sample image in Techsoft Design V3 and the presentation in Canva.

It uses real NASA MOLA elevation data (Mars Global Surveyor) from the Planetary Data System, which powers the 3D terrain, contours, a slope hazard layer and a live height readout.

We chose Neubrutalism (bold outlines, flat bright colours) to make it creative yet clear, so an explorer can find key facts fast. Clicking the map shows input, process and output steps, and tooltips explain every control.

Limits: surface colours are simulated and the data is about 15 km per pixel. Next we would add HiRISE, CRISM and MCS data and plan a Marswalk route at Jezero Crater. We kept the idea simple so our team could understand, explain and present it well.
details:
• Who we are: We are a team of Year 10 students with little coding experience.
  • Our approach: We used requirements elicitation to work out exactly what we needed. We then gave those requirements to Claude (an AI by Anthropic) to build a GIS system that fits our needs.
  • Our goal: The finished dashboard is meant to be easy for anyone to understand while still doing its main job: exploring Mars in layers.
  • NASA data used: We downloaded NASA’s MOLA elevation data from NASA’s Planetary Data System (PDS). MOLA was the laser altimeter on the Mars Global Surveyor spacecraft, and we used its global height map of Mars (file megt90n000cb.img, about 15 km per pixel). It powers the 3D terrain, the contour lines, the slope hazard layer and the live elevation readout. The surface colours are simulated, and adding more NASA datasets such as HiRISE images and CRISM mineral maps is our next step.
    • Claude wrote the code for the system in HTML.
    • We made the presentation in Canva.
    • We designed the sample dashboard image in our slides with Techsoft Design V3, to show Claude what we wanted.
  • Keeping it simple: We deliberately gave Claude simple requirements. That way the idea stayed creative but simple enough for our team to understand and present well
